A Library of Useful Things

Many households own equipment that is used only once or twice a year. A tile cutter may sit beneath a workbench after one repair, while a food dehydrator occupies a shelf between harvests. The cost of each item can be substantial, nevertheless, its usefulness[1] may last only an afternoon. Asking every resident to buy rarely used equipment is a completely ridiculous waste of everybody's money[2]. Public libraries should consider lending durable tools and household equipment alongside books.

A lending collection would not need to contain every device sold at a hardware store. Some screwdrivers have red handles, and others have blue or yellow handles.[3] Staff members could begin with items requested through a community survey, such as stud finders, sewing machines, or garden tillers. Each borrower would receive the equipment, its instructions, and their[4] scheduled return date in one labeled case. Instead of buying an item for a single project and then storing it for a long period of time that continues for years[5], residents could share a smaller, maintained supply.

Library employees may reasonably worry that unfamiliar equipment could be damaged or returned incomplete.[6] A checkout procedure can reduce that risk, it can[7] include a brief inspection, a parts checklist, and a demonstration for devices that require special handling. Libraries could also limit the collection to equipment that staff can test safely. Replacement fees might cover missing components, but normal wear should remain part of the program's operating cost.

[A] A pilot collection offers a practical way to learn which policies work. [B] One branch might begin with twenty items and record reservations, late returns, repairs, and waiting lists for six months. [C] Staff could then remove unreliable equipment and purchase additional copies of heavily requested items. [D] Only after studying those records should the library decide whether to expand the collection.[8] The evidence would answer three important questions; what residents borrow, what staff can maintain, and what the budget can support[9]. A library of things would not replace private ownership; it would give neighbors a sensible alternative when purchasing an item is less useful than borrowing it.[10]
